result:
The question assumes that more agents always give better results, and that isn't true. So neither five nor ten is the right starting point.

Here is why the assumption is tempting. A team of specialists sounds better than one generalist. But every agent is its own loop of model calls, and each call costs tokens. Splitting the work also means agents have to pass information to each other, and each handoff can drop details. Anthropic's write-up on its multi-agent research system reported that agents use roughly 4× the tokens of a plain chat, and multi-agent setups roughly 15×. Check that figure at the source before you quote it at your design review. Your budget is small, so that multiplier matters.

Take a concrete request: "Book me the laser cutter Friday afternoon, and what settings do I use for 3 mm acrylic?" One agent with three tools can handle it: a manual search, a calendar check and a booking tool. Splitting it into a "manual agent", a "calendar agent" and a "booking agent" adds a coordinator on top. The student's request has to be summarized for each of them, and their answers have to be summarized back. You pay for more calls and risk losing details, such as which student or which time slot, and you gain very little.

Splitting pays off when:
- the subtasks are independent and can run in parallel,
- one agent's context would get too big or cluttered with everything,
- or the tools differ so much that one agent gets confused choosing among them.

Your assistant has three tools and mostly sequential steps, so I'd start with one agent. Make the parts that never vary a fixed workflow, such as the booking steps once the slot is confirmed. Add a second agent only if you can name the specific problem the first one has.

Quick check: for the Friday laser-cutter request, which of the three reasons above, if any, would justify splitting? Tell me why in your own words.

If you'd like, I can turn this into a 15-minute lesson on when to split into several agents.
